title: Security architecture and threat modeling
objectives: Place security architecture under Well-Architected Trusted: secure, compliant, and reliable—not MFA folklore alone.
Threat-model a Salesforce design by naming actors, assets, abuse paths, and controls across identity, session, data, and detection.
Keep object permissions, field-level security, and record sharing as separate layers; threat modeling does not collapse them.
Refuse production experiments and real personal data while scoring threats on a LAB_ design.
diagnostic_question: A LAB_ partner community user, an integration user, and an admin automation will all touch the same Case. Before reading, which threats do you name first—stolen session, over-broad sharing, unencrypted field, or missing monitoring—and what evidence would change the order?
definition: Salesforce security architecture is the designed set of controls that keep a solution Trusted: only approved users and systems gain access, they receive only what they need, and data is protected. Well-Architected Secure groups organizational security (authentication and authorization), session and device controls, threat detection and response, sharing and visibility, and encryption. Threat modeling in this lesson is the structured habit of listing actors, assets, abuse paths, and compensating controls before you pick a feature. ([Trusted Overview](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/trusted-overview); [Secure](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/secure); [Data Access](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_data_access.htm))
why_it_matters: Interviewers listen for layered thinking: identity is not authorization, sharing is not FLS, and a pentest checklist is not a threat model. A design that 'has MFA' can still leak records through an integration user or a Public Read/Write object. Trusted Overview asks what data moves, whether Salesforce is a system of record, and how much risk the business will accept—before you draw a sharing diagram.
sixty_second_explanation: Treat the org like a stadium on event day. Authentication is proving the ticket is real. Authorization is which section and which gates your pass opens. Session security is how long the wristband stays valid if you leave and return. Sharing and FLS are which seats and which clipboard fields you can see. Threat modeling is walking the building asking who could sneak in, steal a wristband, overhear a radio, or abuse a vendor pass—and which camera (detection) would notice. Encryption is the locked cash office, not a substitute for the ticket check.
deeper_explanation: A Trusted solution is secure, compliant, and reliable. Secure architectures ensure only approved users gain access, restrict access to what is essential, and protect data from compromise. Trusted planning asks about risk tolerance, data types, system-of-record role, regulations, and whether Salesforce is business-critical. ([Trusted Overview](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/trusted-overview))

Well-Architected Secure points architects at Salesforce built-in features and at context: geography, industry, operating procedures, and customer data types. Under Data Security it lists organizational security (authentication, authorization), session management, device access, threat detection and response, sharing and visibility, and encryption. ([Secure](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/secure))

Help on data access separates what a user can do with an object (object permissions), which fields they can see or edit (field-level security), and which records they can open (sharing). Threat modeling that ignores one layer produces false confidence. ([Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_data_access.htm))

This lesson's threat-model method is Salesforce-aligned, not a claim that STRIDE is a Salesforce product: for each actor (user, community, integration, admin), name the asset (record, field, session, API), the abuse (impersonation, over-access, exfiltration, integrity loss), and the control (identity, authorization, sharing, encryption, monitoring). Do not invent that Event Monitoring or a named Shield SKU is entitled in every org—verify licenses.

Security architecture is design metadata: permission sets, sharing, named credentials, encryption settings. The Cases those controls protect are business data. Do not 'test' a threat by opening production sharing.

mental_model.analogy: A stadium on event day: ticket check is authentication; section pass is authorization; wristband timeout is session security; seats and clipboards are record and field access; walking the building for sneak-ins, stolen wristbands, and vendor-pass abuse is threat modeling; cameras are detection; the locked cash office is encryption.
useful_mapping: authentication → proving the ticket is genuine
authorization / object permissions → which gates your pass opens
field-level security → which clipboard fields you may read or write
sharing / visibility → which seats you may reach
session and device → wristband lifetime and which turnstiles accept it
threat modeling → named actors, assets, abuse paths, and controls
threat detection → cameras and radios after a control fails
where_it_breaks: A stadium has one perimeter; Salesforce has org, user, and data layers plus API and community surfaces the analogy under-draws.
Encryption is not a substitute for sharing; a locked office still needs a ticket check.
Named monitoring products are license-gated; do not assume every org has the same cameras.
Compliance (legal, ethical, accessibility) sits beside Secure under Trusted and is not a turnstile.

teach_back_prompt: Walk a teammate through authentication, authorization, sharing, FLS, session, and threat modeling using the stadium, then name one place the analogy breaks.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory, list Secure's organizational, session, detection, sharing, and encryption concerns.
Threat-model a LAB_ integration user: actor, asset, abuse, control.
Explain why MFA does not fix Public Read/Write on a sensitive object.
Separate object permission, FLS, and sharing for a Case a partner user should not see.
Two-minute interview: Trusted Secure plus a four-part threat model, no product dump.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Security architecture is how a Salesforce solution stays Trusted: prove identity, grant least capability, share the right records, protect fields, and detect abuse. Threat modeling names actor, asset, abuse, and control before I pick a feature.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I start from Trusted planning: data class, system of record, risk. I separate authentication from authorization, then object permission, FLS, and sharing. I add session, encryption, and detection. I do not claim Shield products without a license check. I never test a threat in production or with real personal data.

terminology.plain: The planned layers that keep the org Trusted, not a single checkbox.
terminology.precise: The designed combination of identity, authorization, session, sharing and visibility, encryption, and detection that matches data class and risk—using Salesforce built-in features in context.
terminology.example: A LAB_ Case design that names partner users, integration users, FLS on a government-id field, and Private OWD before go-live.
terminology.non_example: Turning on MFA and declaring the architecture complete.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: A penetration-test report: evidence of residual risk, not the architecture itself.
terminology.boundary: OWD and sharing-rule mechanics are SEC-004 territory; this lesson is the architect's threat-informed map.

terminology.plain: Walking the design asking who could abuse what, before you build.
terminology.precise: A structured pass over actors, assets, abuse paths, and controls aligned to Trusted Secure (identity, session, data, detection). This handbook does not claim a Salesforce product named STRIDE.
terminology.example: Integration user with Modify All on LAB_Case: abuse is bulk exfiltration; control is least-privilege named credential plus monitoring.
terminology.non_example: A generic 'hackers exist' slide with no actor or asset.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Threat detection: cameras after the fact, not the design-time model.
terminology.boundary: Do not run exploit proofs; architecture interviews want controls, not attack recipes.

terminology.plain: Proving the actor is who they claim.
terminology.precise: Organizational security's identity proof (and MFA where required). Necessary for Trusted Secure, not sufficient for authorization or sharing.
terminology.example: SSO plus MFA for employees entering the LAB_ org.
terminology.non_example: A permission set that grants Case edit—that is authorization.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Session security: keeping a proven identity bound to a time-limited session.
terminology.boundary: Identity provider mechanics are SEC-001; here it is one threat-model node.

terminology.plain: What a proven actor is allowed to do.
terminology.precise: Capability grants such as object permissions (and, with FLS, field capability). Distinct from which records sharing exposes.
terminology.example: Partner profile can Read LAB_Case but FLS hides a sensitive field.
terminology.non_example: OWD Private—that is record sharing, not object capability.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Record sharing: which rows, after object permission exists.
terminology.boundary: Permission set groups and muting are later SEC; this lesson needs the layer split.

terminology.plain: Which records an authorized user can actually open.
terminology.precise: The record-access stack above object permission: organization-wide defaults and the sharing layers that can widen them. A Secure concern under Trusted.
terminology.example: Private LAB_Case OWD plus a sharing rule for the on-call group.
terminology.non_example: Hiding a field with FLS and calling it record sharing.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Restriction rules (neighboring SEC): additional limits, not this lesson's full catalog.
terminology.boundary: Do not collapse OWD into threat modeling as the only control.

terminology.plain: Noticing and reacting when a control fails.
terminology.precise: A Well-Architected Secure concern covering detection and response. Specific Event Monitoring or Shield capabilities are license-sensitive (Needs verification per org).
terminology.example: Alerting when the LAB_ integration user downloads an unusual volume of Cases—if the org's monitoring entitlement allows it.
terminology.non_example: Assuming every org has the same camera product.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Threat modeling: design-time questions, not the runtime feed.
terminology.boundary: Quote current Help for the named product; do not invent event types.

when_to_use: When an interview asks you to describe Salesforce security architecture and how you threat-model a design.
When a new community, integration user, or sensitive field is added and Trusted Secure must be scored before build.
When a team treats MFA as the entire security architecture and skips object permission, FLS, or sharing.
When you must separate detection (runtime) from threat modeling (design-time) and verify monitoring licenses.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this security-architecture lesson as a substitute for OWD and sharing-rule mechanics (SEC-004).
Do not treat encryption as a replacement for sharing and FLS, or invent that every org includes Shield.
Do not run exploit proofs, password attacks, or production sharing experiments as 'threat modeling.'
Do not collapse authentication into authorization, or object permission into record access.

Named credentials and integration users as first-class actors.

hands_on_lab.environment: Document plus optional disposable sandbox; synthetic LAB_ names only.
starting_state_checks: You can open Trusted Overview and Control Who Sees What.
You will not change production sharing or identity settings.

For each actor, fill asset, abuse, and control across identity, object permission, FLS, sharing, and session.

Write one sentence on where the stadium analogy breaks for API integrations.

decision_table.signal: The debate is whether the person is really that user or app.
decision_table.choose: Treat it as authentication and session/device security.
decision_table.not: Add a sharing rule or a new field as if that proved identity.
decision_table.why: Trusted Secure separates authentication and session management from sharing and visibility.

decision_table.signal: The actor is known but can use the wrong object or field.
decision_table.choose: Fix object permissions and field-level security as distinct layers.
decision_table.not: Tighten OWD only, or hide the tab and call it FLS.
decision_table.why: Control Who Sees What documents object, field, and record access separately.

decision_table.signal: The actor should use the object but only some rows.
decision_table.choose: Design sharing and visibility (OWD plus widening layers) after object permission exists.
decision_table.not: Grant Modify All Data to skip sharing design.
decision_table.why: Secure architectures restrict access to what is essential; Modify All is an abuse path in a threat model.

decision_table.signal: Sensitive data at rest, in files, or on an integration wire is the asset.
decision_table.choose: Classify first, then consider encryption, named credentials, and field exposure; verify licenses.
decision_table.not: Assume Shield Platform Encryption exists in every org, or use encryption as a sharing substitute.
decision_table.why: Secure tells architects to consider data types and built-in features in context; entitlements vary.

decision_table.signal: You need to know when a control failed.
decision_table.choose: Plan threat detection and response with org-verified tools.
decision_table.not: Confuse detection with design-time threat modeling, or invent event types.
decision_table.why: Detection is a Secure family of its own; modeling is the four-part table you write before build.

limitations: Does not replace SEC sharing-feature catalogs.
Does not list every Shield or Event Monitoring event.
Guest, Experience Cloud, and mobile device specifics need current Help.
No exploit instructions; interviews want controls.
security_notes: Never use real personal data in LAB_ threat models.
Do not open production sharing to 'see what happens.'
Integration users are high-value actors; least privilege is the default design.
common_mistakes: Collapsing FLS into sharing or sharing into object permission.
Encryption as a substitute for who can query the row.

troubleshooting.symptom: A user authenticates but cannot open a record.
check: Not FLS if the whole record is missing

troubleshooting.symptom: A user opens the record but a field is missing.
An integration exports more Cases than the design allowed.

Whether detection exists in this org

production_notes: Keep the threat-model table with the design; revisit when actors change.
License-check detection and encryption before go-live claims.
No production identity or sharing experiments from this lesson.

interview_questions.question: What is Salesforce security architecture in Well-Architected language?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: It is how the solution stays Trusted: secure, compliant, and reliable. Secure means approved, least-essential access and protected data—not MFA alone.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start from Trusted planning: data class, system of record, regulations, criticality. I map Secure families: identity, authorization, session, sharing, encryption, detection. I split object permission, FLS, and record sharing. I verify licenses before naming Shield or Event Monitoring. I keep controls as metadata and Cases as data.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ Case with partner, employee, and integration actors scored before a field is created.
tradeoffs: Speed of delivery vs Trusted completeness
Broad integration access vs least privilege
weak_answer_warnings: Using a generic catalog metaphor instead of layered access

interview_questions.question: How do you threat-model a Salesforce design in an interview?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I list actors, assets, abuse paths, and controls. I walk identity, session, object, field, sharing, encryption, and detection. I do not claim STRIDE is a Salesforce product.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Employee, community, integration, and admin are different tickets. For each I ask what they could steal, alter, or over-read. I match a control to a layer rather than stacking slogans. Detection is what we do after a control fails, and it may be license-gated. I will not describe exploits.
interview_questions.example: Integration user + LAB_Case + bulk export + least privilege and monitoring gap noted.
follow_ups: What if the actor is a guest user?
How do named credentials change the model?

interview_questions.question: MFA is on. Ship a partner community on Public Read/Write Case?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: No. Authentication is not sharing. I threat-model partner over-read, set object permission and OWD deliberately, and hide sensitive fields with FLS.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Trusted planning asks what data partners see. Public Read/Write is an abuse path, not collaboration magic. I separate Experience Cloud identity from employee SSO. I would rather a Private OWD plus a sharing path than a stadium with no section ropes. I do not invent guest defaults; I would verify current community sharing Help.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ advisor community on Case with Private OWD and a sharing set or rule—exact community feature Needs verification in the org.
tradeoffs: One OWD vs extra sharing metadata
follow_ups: What field must partners never see?
weak_answer_warnings: MFA as sufficient for community data

interview_questions.question: The middleware team wants the integration user to have Modify All Data. Respond.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I threat-model bulk exfiltration and integrity loss. Modify All is not an integration pattern. We grant essential objects and use named credentials.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Secure says restrict to what is essential. I would also ask whether the API runs as a dedicated user, whether connected-app scopes are tight, and whether detection exists in this org. MFA on a human admin is the wrong ticket. Secrets do not go in Case comments. ARCH-006 will add failure modes; this lesson is the actor.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ upsert user with CRUD on LAB_Case only, no View All Data.
tradeoffs: One god user vs several scoped users
follow_ups: With sharing versus without sharing in Apex?
How do you rotate the credential?
weak_answer_warnings: Approving Modify All to 'make the API work'

interview_questions.question: A user logs in but cannot open a Case another user sees. How do you walk the layers?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Identity already worked. Check object permission, then record sharing, then layout. Do not start at encryption or MFA.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Control Who Sees What is the script: object, field, record. If the record is missing, FLS is the wrong first stop. If the record opens and a field is missing, then FLS and layout. I also check whether they are a community user with a different sharing model. I would not change production OWD to debug.

tradeoffs: Debug in sandbox vs production peek
Sharing fix vs accidental View All
follow_ups: How do you prove sharing in a query?
Could a restriction rule be in play? (Neighboring SEC.)
weak_answer_warnings: Resetting the password first as the only step

interview_questions.question: Leadership wants encryption 'instead of sharing' because of an audit. Answer.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Encryption is a Secure family, not a sharing substitute. Auditors still care who can query the row. Classify data, then layer sharing and encryption, and verify licenses.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Trusted lists sharing and encryption separately. I would ask which data class triggered the audit. Platform Encryption, if entitled, has limitations that must be read from current Help—Needs verification, I will not invent which fields can be encrypted. Easy still asks who can maintain the model. I refuse a single toggle story.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ government-id field: FLS plus Private OWD, encryption only if entitled and suitable.
tradeoffs: Encryption operational cost vs sharing design
follow_ups: What cannot be encrypted? (Cite current Help.)

interview_questions.question: Where does threat detection sit, and what must you verify?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Detection is runtime noticing and response, a Secure family. I verify org entitlements before naming Event Monitoring or other products.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Modeling without detection leaves failed controls invisible. Detection without modeling is a camera pointed at the wrong gate. I write the abuse first, then ask whether this org can see that event. If not, I record a gap rather than invent logs. I still would not skip sharing because 'we will watch it.'
interview_questions.example: Unusual export by LAB_ integration user—capability Needs verification in the org.
follow_ups: How does this meet Adaptable incident response?
weak_answer_warnings: Listing SKUs with no license check

interview_questions.question: Teach security architecture with the stadium, then break the analogy.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Tickets are authentication, sections are authorization, seats are sharing, clipboards are FLS, wristbands are sessions, walking for sneak-ins is threat modeling, cameras are detection, cash office is encryption. APIs and licenses break the picture.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I map a LAB_ Case through four actors. I say compliance is not a turnstile. I forbid production experiments and real student data. I remind them encryption is not a ticket check. I finish with object, field, and record as three gates so Help's data-access split is audible.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ university partner advisors plus integration upsert.
tradeoffs: Memorable analogy vs extra Salesforce surfaces
follow_ups: Where do named credentials sit in the stadium?
